card.definition: "Your" means it belongs to you. "You're" is a short way to say "you are." The mark in "you're" takes the place of the letter a.

using-simple-tenses.title: Using Action Verbs in Simple Tenses

card.definition: Verbs change to show when an action happens. "Today" means it happens now. "Yesterday" means it already happened. "Tomorrow" means it will happen later.

example.text: Today Sam walks to school. Yesterday Sam walked to school. Tomorrow Sam will walk to school.
example.note: Walks is now. Walked is past. Will walk is later.

card.how: The word that tells when, like today or yesterday, helps you pick the right verb form.

Today Leo plays. Tomorrow Leo will play.

card.definition: A compound sentence joins two complete thoughts with a word like and, but, or so. Each part could stand alone as a sentence.

example.text: The rain stopped, and the sun came out.

complex-sentences.title: Adding Ideas with a Middle Connecting Word
complex-sentences.ask: Choose the sentence that adds the extra idea the right way.

card.definition: A complex sentence adds an extra idea to a main thought with a connecting word in the middle, like because, when, or after. The extra idea cannot stand alone.

example.text: We stayed inside because it was raining.

more.note: is the main thought.
adds the reason.

card.how: Because connects the reason to the main thought.

tips.text: Sam smiled when he saw his friend.
We packed our bags after lunch.

items.text: The garden grew. It rained all week.
items.prompt: The garden grew. It rained all week.
options: The garden grew although it rained all week.
The garden grew, it rained all week.
The garden grew because it rained all week.
The garden grew. Because it rained all week.
items.right: The garden grew because it rained all week.
items.hint: Rain all week is the reason the garden grew. Pick the connecting word that gives a reason.

items.text: Leo ran to the door. He heard the bell.

items.right: Leo ran to the door when he heard the bell.
items.hint: Hearing the bell tells the moment Leo ran. Pick the connecting word that tells the time.

card.definition: A coordinating conjunction is a small word that joins two words, phrases, or thoughts. The main ones are and, but, or, so, for, nor, and yet.

example.text: We wanted to play outside, but it was raining.
example.note: But joins the two thoughts.

card.how: But shows that the second thought is different from the first.

items.text: The cat slept and the dog played.
items.hint: Look for the small word that joins what the cat did with what the dog did.

items.text: We can swim or we can hike.
items.hint: Look for the small word that gives a choice.

items.text: It was late, so we went home.
items.hint: Look for the small word that joins a cause with what happened next.

items.text: Leo likes soccer, but he does not like tennis.
items.hint: Look for the small word that joins two different thoughts.

items.text: The soup was hot, yet Sam ate it all.
items.hint: Look for the small word that joins two thoughts that seem to disagree.

items.text: We stayed inside, for it was snowing.
items.hint: Look for the small word that joins a reason to a thought.

items.text: Mia did not want cake, nor did she want pie.
items.hint: Look for the small word that joins two things that are both not wanted.

items.text: Ana read a book and wrote a story.
items.hint: Look for the small word that joins two things Ana did.

items.text: You can have juice or milk.
items.hint: Look for the small word that gives a choice between two drinks.

items.text: The baby was tired, so she slept.
items.hint: Look for the small word that shows what happened because the baby was tired.

items.text: Sam is small, but he is strong.
items.hint: Look for the small word that joins two different ideas.

items.text: We packed sandwiches, and we packed fruit.
items.hint: Look for the small word that joins the two things we packed.

sections.title: Facts
sections.question: What is a fact?

passage.text: Bees help flowers grow by moving pollen from one flower to another.
A single hive can hold 50,000 bees.

sections.note: Both sentences are facts, because both can be checked. The second one also gives a number.

sections.title: Matching evidence
sections.question: Does the fact fit the point?

passage.text: Bees are important to farms.
A single hive can hold 50,000 bees.
Bees help flowers grow by moving pollen.

sections.note: The sentence about pollen fits the point about farms. It explains why bees matter to farmers.

sections.title: Strong vs. weak
sections.question: Which fact is stronger?

passage.text: Bees are important to farms.
Bees are nice.
A farm with bees grows more food.

sections.note: The sentence about growing more food is stronger evidence. It connects bees to what farms do.

recognizing-fragments.title: Recognizing Fragments

card.definition: A fragment is a group of words that is not a complete sentence. It is missing a subject, a verb, or a complete thought.

avoiding-run-ons.title: Avoiding Run-Ons
avoiding-run-ons.ask: Fix the run-on. Any right fix counts.

card.definition: A run-on is two complete sentences joined with no punctuation or joining word. Fix it by splitting it into two sentences or by joining it with a comma and a word like and, but, or so.

example.text: The sun came out we went outside.
example.note: This is a run-on. Fix it like this:

then.text: The sun came out, and we went outside.

card.how: The comma and the word and join the two complete thoughts the right way.

then.text: Sam was hungry, so he ate a sandwich.

evidence-that-supports.title: Which Pieces of Evidence Support the Opinion?
evidence-that-supports.ask: Tap the sentence that supports the opinion.

sections.title: Opinions and facts
sections.question: What makes a fact good evidence?

passage.text: Dogs make great pets.
Dogs are loyal and love to play.
I like dogs.

sections.note: The sentence about loyalty supports the opinion. The sentence about liking dogs does not.

sections.title: Checking the fit
sections.question: Does the fact match the opinion?

Gardens teach students where food comes from.
The garden has a fence.

sections.note: The sentence about where food comes from matches the opinion. The sentence about the fence does not.

Riding a bike keeps you healthy and costs nothing.
Bikes have wheels.

progressive-verbs.title: Using Progressive Verbs
progressive-verbs.ask: Press the verb to choose the form that fits.

card.definition: A progressive verb shows an action that is happening right now or was happening over time. It uses a form of be plus a verb that ends in ing.

example.text: Sam is reading a book.
example.note: Is reading shows the action is happening now.

card.how: Is plus reading makes the progressive form.

tips.text: Ana was singing when the phone rang.
tips.note: Was singing shows the action was happening over time.

tips.text: The dogs are barking at the mail truck.
tips.note: Are barking shows the action is happening now.

items.right: Sam is reading a book right now.
items.hint: Right now tells you the action is still going on. Pick the verb that shows it in progress.

items.right: Ana was singing when the phone rang.
items.hint: The singing was going on when the phone rang. Pick the verb that shows it was in progress.

card.definition: A sentence should keep the same verb tense unless the time really changes. A tense shift is when the verbs jump from one time to another for no reason.

example.note: Walked is past, but buys is present. Fix it:

active-or-passive.title: Is the Sentence Active or Passive?
active-or-passive.ask: Is the sentence active or passive?

card.definition: A sentence is active when the subject does the action. A sentence is passive when the subject receives the action, and the verb usually follows a form of be plus a past participle.

example.text: Ana painted the fence.
example.note: Passive:

then.text: The fence was painted by Ana.
then.note: In the passive sentence, the fence receives the action.

card.how: Find the subject. If the subject does the action, the sentence is active. If the action happens to the subject, it is passive.

tips.note: Active, the cook does the tasting.

tips.text: The soup was tasted by the cook.
tips.note: Passive, the soup receives the action.

card.definition: Articles are the words a, an, and the. They come before a noun and tell whether the noun is general or specific.

sections.title: What a claim is
sections.question: What is the writer trying to prove?
sections.body: A claim is the main opinion in a paragraph. It is a statement the writer must support with facts and reasons.

passage.text: Schools should keep art classes.
Art helps students think in new ways, and it gives every student a chance to shine.

sections.note: The claim is the first sentence. It states the opinion the paragraph will prove.

sections.title: What makes a claim strong
sections.question: Is the claim clear and debatable?
sections.body: A strong claim is clear, specific, and something a reasonable person could disagree with.

passage.text: Recess should last 30 minutes.

sections.note: This claim is clear and specific, and someone could argue for a different length. A weak claim would be “Recess is nice,” which is vague and hard to argue about.

sections.title: Claims in a paragraph
sections.question: Where does the claim belong?
sections.body: The claim usually comes first, as the topic sentence, and the rest of the paragraph supports it.

passage.text: Every student should learn to swim.
Swimming is a life skill, pools are open all year, and lessons are safe with a trained teacher.

sections.note: The claim opens the paragraph, and the sentences after it give reasons.

items.text: Schools should keep art classes. Art helps students think in new ways, and it gives every student a chance to shine.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: Art helps students think in new ways, and it gives every student a chance to shine.
items.right: Schools should keep art classes.
items.hint: The claim is the opinion the paragraph will prove.

items.text: The town needs a new library. The old one is too small for the crowds on weekends. A bigger library would hold more books and more computers.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: The town needs a new library.
The old one is too small for the crowds on weekends.
A bigger library would hold more books and more computers.
items.right: The town needs a new library.
items.hint: The claim states what the writer thinks should happen.

items.text: Every family with a yard should consider adopting a dog from the shelter.
items.ask: Which is the stronger claim?
options: Every family with a yard should consider adopting a dog from the shelter.
items.right: Every family with a yard should consider adopting a dog from the shelter.
items.hint: A strong claim is clear, specific, and debatable.

items.text: The school garden should grow food for the cafeteria.
items.ask: Which is the stronger claim?
options: The school garden is the best garden.
The school garden should grow food for the cafeteria.
items.right: The school garden should grow food for the cafeteria.
items.hint: A strong claim is specific and can be supported with reasons.

items.text: Homework should be shorter on Fridays. Students are tired by the end of the week. Shorter homework would still cover the key ideas.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: Homework should be shorter on Fridays.
Students are tired by the end of the week.
Shorter homework would still cover the key ideas.
items.right: Homework should be shorter on Fridays.
items.hint: Find the sentence that the other sentences support.

items.text: Evening games end in the dark. Players cannot see the ball after sunset. The soccer field needs new lights.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: Evening games end in the dark.
Players cannot see the ball after sunset.
The soccer field needs new lights.
items.right: The soccer field needs new lights.
items.hint: The claim is the opinion the writer wants to prove.

items.text: Every classroom should have a shelf of books students can borrow.
items.ask: Which is the stronger claim?
options: Every classroom should have a shelf of books students can borrow.
items.right: Every classroom should have a shelf of books students can borrow.
items.hint: A strong claim is clear and specific, not vague.

items.text: The park should add a skate ramp. Many students ride skateboards after school. A ramp would give them a safe place to practice.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: The park should add a skate ramp.
Many students ride skateboards after school.
A ramp would give them a safe place to practice.
items.right: The park should add a skate ramp.
items.hint: Ask which sentence gives an opinion and which sentences give reasons.

items.text: Music class should meet twice a week so students can practice their instruments.
items.ask: Which is the stronger claim?
options: Music class should meet twice a week so students can practice their instruments.
items.right: Music class should meet twice a week so students can practice their instruments.
items.hint: A strong claim names something specific that can be argued about.

items.text: Fresh fruit is healthy and easy to eat. The cafeteria should serve fresh fruit every day. Students would choose it over chips.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: Fresh fruit is healthy and easy to eat.
The cafeteria should serve fresh fruit every day.
Students would choose it over chips.
items.right: The cafeteria should serve fresh fruit every day.
items.hint: The claim states the opinion the paragraph will prove.

items.text: Libraries are great.
items.ask: Which is the weaker claim?
options: The library should stay open later.
items.right: Libraries are great.
items.hint: A weak claim is vague and hard to support with reasons.

items.text: Bikes should be allowed on the path by the river. The path is wide enough for walkers and riders. Signs would keep everyone safe.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: Bikes should be allowed on the path by the river.
The path is wide enough for walkers and riders.
items.right: Bikes should be allowed on the path by the river.

claims-evidence-reasoning.title: Identifying Claims, Evidence, and Reasoning
claims-evidence-reasoning.ask: Tap the sentence that does the job.

sections.title: Claims
sections.question: What is the writer trying to prove?
sections.body: A claim is the opinion the writer wants to prove.

passage.text: Our school should start classes later in the morning.
Students learn better when they are rested, and a later start would help everyone focus.

sections.note: The claim is the first sentence. It states the opinion the paragraph will prove.

sections.title: Evidence
sections.question: What fact backs up the claim?
sections.body: Evidence is a fact, an example, or a quote that supports the claim.

passage.text: A study of 200 schools found that students scored higher on morning tests after start times moved later.

sections.note: The evidence is the sentence with the study result. It gives a fact that supports the claim.

sections.title: Reasoning
sections.question: How does the evidence connect to the claim?
sections.body: Reasoning explains why the evidence matters and how it proves the claim.

passage.text: When students sleep longer, they pay attention in class, so later start times lead to better learning.

sections.note: The reasoning is the sentence that links the fact to the claim. It explains why the evidence matters.

items.text: The town library should stay open on Sundays. A survey found that many families can visit the library only on weekends. Opening on Sundays would let those families use the library when they are free.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: The town library should stay open on Sundays.
A survey found that many families can visit the library only on weekends.
Opening on Sundays would let those families use the library when they are free.
items.right: The town library should stay open on Sundays.
items.hint: The claim is the opinion the writer wants to prove.

items.text: The town library should stay open on Sundays. A survey found that many families can visit the library only on weekends. Opening on Sundays would let those families use the library when they are free.

A survey found that many families can visit the library only on weekends.
Opening on Sundays would let those families use the library when they are free.
items.right: A survey found that many families can visit the library only on weekends.
items.hint: Evidence is a fact that backs up the claim.

items.text: Recess should be longer. Children who play outside every day concentrate better in class. A longer break gives them time to run, play, and return ready to learn.
items.ask: Which sentence is the reasoning?
options: Children who play outside every day concentrate better in class.
A longer break gives them time to run, play, and return ready to learn.
items.right: A longer break gives them time to run, play, and return ready to learn.
items.hint: Reasoning explains how the evidence connects to the claim.

items.text: Every student should learn to cook a simple meal. Cooking teaches planning and measuring. A school cooking club met once a week and members cooked lunch for their class.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: Every student should learn to cook a simple meal.
A school cooking club met once a week and members cooked lunch for their class.
items.right: Every student should learn to cook a simple meal.
items.hint: The claim states what the writer thinks should happen.

items.text: Every student should learn to cook a simple meal. Cooking teaches planning and measuring. A school cooking club met once a week and members cooked lunch for their class.
items.ask: Which sentence is evidence?
options: Every student should learn to cook a simple meal.
A school cooking club met once a week and members cooked lunch for their class.
items.right: A school cooking club met once a week and members cooked lunch for their class.
items.hint: Evidence is something that actually happened, a fact that supports the claim.

items.text: The class trip to the river taught us more than any textbook. We measured the water, counted the fish, and wrote down what we saw. Doing the work ourselves made the science stick.
items.ask: Which sentence is the reasoning?
options: The class trip to the river taught us more than any textbook.

Doing the work ourselves made the science stick.
items.right: Doing the work ourselves made the science stick.
items.hint: Reasoning says why the evidence matters for the claim.

items.right: The school should plant a vegetable garden.

literary-context.title: Context for Literary Evidence: Speaker, Listener, and Plot Clue

sections.title: What context is
sections.question: What does the reader need to know before the quote?
sections.body: Context is the background a reader needs to understand a piece of evidence from a story. It names who is speaking, who is listening, and what is happening in the plot.

passage.text: In the chapter where the young sailor first meets the captain, the sailor says, 'I have never seen a storm like this.'

sections.note: The context tells us the speaker is the sailor, the listener is the captain, and the plot moment is their first meeting.

sections.title: Why the speaker and listener matter
sections.question: Who says it, and to whom?
sections.body: Knowing the speaker and listener helps the reader judge what the words mean.

passage.text: When the teacher asks the class why the bridge fell, one student answers, 'The wood was rotten.'

sections.note: The speaker is a student, the listener is the teacher, and that tells us the words are an answer to a question.

sections.title: Why the plot clue matters
sections.question: What is happening in the story at this moment?
sections.body: A plot clue places the quote in the story so the reader can follow it.

passage.text: Just after the storm destroys the barn, the farmer looks at the field and says, 'We will rebuild.'

sections.note: The plot clue is the storm destroying the barn, and it explains why the farmer speaks of rebuilding.

nonfiction-context.title: Context for Nonfiction Evidence: Source Information and Reporting Verbs

sections.title: What source information is
sections.question: Where did this fact come from?
sections.body: Source information tells the reader who wrote or said the fact and where it was published, so the reader can judge whether to trust it.

passage.text: Dr. Patel, a scientist who studies oceans, writes in her 2024 book that sea levels are rising.

sections.note: The source information is Dr. Patel, a scientist who studies oceans, and her 2024 book.

sections.title: Reporting verbs
sections.question: Which verb introduces the fact?
sections.body: A reporting verb such as states, explains, notes, or warns introduces a fact from a source. The verb you choose shapes how the reader hears the fact.

passage.text: The report warns that the river is polluted.

sections.note: Warns tells the reader the fact is serious. “The report notes that the river is polluted.” Notes tells the reader the fact is simply stated.

sections.title: Putting them together
sections.question: How do source information and a reporting verb work together?
sections.body: Together they let the reader know who said it and how strongly it was said.

passage.text: In her guide to city parks, ranger Ana Lopez explains that the new trail is safe for families.

sections.note: The source is ranger Ana Lopez and her guide, and explains introduces the fact in a calm, clear way.

sections.title: What a paraphrase is
sections.question: What does it mean to put an idea in your own words?
sections.body: A paraphrase restates someone else's idea using your own words and your own sentence structure. It is not a copy with a few words swapped.

passage.label: Original
passage.text: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, which helps plants make seeds.

passage.label: Good paraphrase
passage.text: When bees move pollen between flowers, plants can produce seeds.

sections.note: The idea is the same, but the words and the sentence shape are new.

sections.title: What plagiarism looks like
sections.question: When is a restatement too close to the original?
sections.body: Copying a sentence and changing one or two words is still plagiarism.

passage.label: Original
passage.text: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, which helps plants make seeds.

passage.label: Too close
passage.text: Bees carry pollen from bloom to bloom, which helps plants make seeds.

sections.note: Only one word changed, so it is still a copy.

sections.title: How to paraphrase safely
sections.question: How do I make it truly my own?
sections.body: Read the idea, look away, write it in your own words, and name the source.

passage.label: Original
passage.text: The moon has no light of its own.
It shines because it reflects light from the sun.

passage.label: Safe paraphrase
passage.text: Moonlight is really sunlight bouncing off the moon, since the moon does not glow by itself.

sections.note: The words and the shape are new. When you use it in your writing, name the source too.

matching-pronouns-verbs.title: Matching Pronouns and Verbs between Context and Quotations
matching-pronouns-verbs.ask: Choose the sentence that matches the quote.

sections.title: What matching means
sections.question: Why must the words around a quote agree with the quote?
sections.body: When you introduce a quote, the pronouns and verbs in your own sentence must match the pronouns and verbs inside the quote, or the sentence will not make sense.

passage.label: Quote
passage.text: I will finish the poster.

passage.label: Your sentence
passage.text: Maya said that she would finish the poster.

sections.note: She matches I, since both point to Maya, and would finish matches the plan Maya stated. A mismatch would be “Maya said that he would finish the poster,” which changes who does the work.

sections.title: Pronouns
sections.question: Whose words are these?
sections.body: The pronoun in your lead-in must point to the same person as the pronoun in the quote.

passage.label: Quote
passage.text: You played well.

passage.label: Your sentence
passage.text: The coach told the team that they had played well.

sections.note: You in the quote points to the team, so your sentence uses they, not a pronoun for one player.

sections.title: Verbs
sections.question: When did it happen?
sections.body: The verb tense in your lead-in must match the time in the quote.

passage.text: Ana explained that she had read the book.

sections.note: Had read is past, and explained is past, so the times agree. A mismatch would be “Ana explains that she had read the book,” which mixes present and past.

items.prompt: Maya's words: "I will finish the poster."
options: Maya said that she would finish the poster.

items.right: Maya said that she would finish the poster.
items.hint: The pronoun in your sentence must point to the same person as in the quote.

in-text-citations.title: Formatting In-Text Citations
in-text-citations.ask: Choose the citation written the right way.

sections.title: What an in-text citation is
sections.question: How do I show where a fact came from inside my writing?
sections.body: An in-text citation is a short note in parentheses after a fact or quote that names the source.

passage.text: Wolves hunt in packs (Rivera 24).

sections.note: The note in parentheses tells the reader the fact came from Rivera, page 24.

sections.title: Where it goes
sections.question: Where does the citation sit?
sections.body: The citation comes right after the fact or quote, before the period at the end of the sentence.

passage.text: The river is the longest in the state (Lopez 41).

sections.note: The citation sits before the period, not after it.

sections.title: What it contains
sections.question: What goes inside the parentheses?
sections.body: For a book, put the author's last name and the page number, with no comma between them.

passage.text: Bees visit hundreds of flowers in one day (Patel 12).

sections.note: Patel is the author, and 12 is the page.

items.text: Wolves hunt in packs (Rivera 24).
items.ask: Which sentence formats the citation correctly?
items.right: Wolves hunt in packs (Rivera 24).
items.hint: Check where the period sits compared with the parentheses.

items.text: The river is the longest in the state (Lopez 41).
items.ask: Which sentence formats the citation correctly?
options: The river is the longest in the state (Lopez, 41).
The river is the longest in the state (Lopez 41).
items.right: The river is the longest in the state (Lopez 41).
items.hint: Check what sits between the name and the page number.

items.text: Bees visit hundreds of flowers in one day (Patel 12).
items.ask: Which sentence formats the citation correctly?
options: Bees visit hundreds of flowers in one day (Patel 12).

items.right: Bees visit hundreds of flowers in one day (Patel 12).
items.hint: Look closely at what comes before the page number.

items.right: The moon reflects sunlight (Kim 8).

using-transitions.title: Using the Appropriate Transition Words and Phrases

sections.title: What transitions do
sections.question: How do I connect one idea to the next?
sections.body: Transition words and phrases link sentences and show how ideas relate, such as adding, contrasting, or showing cause and effect.

passage.text: The team practiced every day.
As a result, they won the final game.

sections.note: As a result shows that the win followed from the practice.

sections.title: Choosing the right transition
sections.question: Which transition fits the link?
sections.body: For adding an idea, use also, in addition, or furthermore. For contrast, use however, on the other hand, or nevertheless. For cause and effect, use therefore, as a result, or consequently.

passage.text: The rain was heavy.
However, the game went on.

sections.note: However shows a contrast between the rain and the game going on.

sections.title: Where transitions belong
sections.question: Where does the transition sit?
sections.body: A transition usually starts the sentence it connects, followed by a comma.

passage.text: First, the class planned the garden.
Next, they dug the beds.
Finally, they planted the seeds.

sections.note: First, next, and finally show the order of steps.

items.text: The team practiced every day. As a result, they won the final game.
items.right: The team practiced every day. As a result, they won the final game.
items.label: Cause and effect
items.ask: What does as a result show?
items.hint: Ask how winning the final game connects to practicing every day.

items.text: The garden grew tomatoes. ___, it grew peppers.
items.ask: Which transition adds an idea?
items.right: The garden grew tomatoes. in addition, it grew peppers.
items.hint: Ask whether the peppers add to the tomatoes or contrast with them.

items.text: The rain was heavy. ___, the game went on.
items.ask: Which transition shows contrast?
items.right: The rain was heavy. however, the game went on.
items.hint: Ask whether the game going on fits with the heavy rain or goes against it.

items.text: The bus was late. ___, we missed the first class.
items.ask: Which transition shows cause and effect?
items.right: The bus was late. as a result, we missed the first class.
items.hint: Ask whether missing class happened because of the late bus or in contrast to it.

items.text: First, the class planned the garden. Next, they dug the beds. Finally, they planted the seeds.
items.right: First, the class planned the garden. Next, they dug the beds. Finally, they planted the seeds.
items.label: Order of steps
items.ask: What do first, next, and finally show?
items.hint: Ask what first, next, and finally tell you about the steps.

items.text: The movie was long. ___, it was exciting.
items.ask: Which transition fits?
items.right: The movie was long. however, it was exciting.
items.hint: Ask whether exciting goes along with long or goes against it.

items.text: The library is quiet. ___, it has many books.
items.ask: Which transition fits?
items.right: The library is quiet. furthermore, it has many books.
items.hint: Ask whether having many books adds to being quiet or contrasts with it.

items.text: She studied hard. ___, she passed the test.
items.ask: Which transition fits?
items.right: She studied hard. therefore, she passed the test.
items.hint: Ask whether passing happened because of studying or in contrast to it.

items.text: At the start of the sentence it connects, followed by a comma
items.ask: Where does a transition usually sit?
items.prompt: "First, the class planned the garden."
options: At the start of the sentence it connects, followed by a comma
At the start of the sentence, with no comma after it
At the end of the sentence, after the period
items.right: At the start of the sentence it connects, followed by a comma
items.hint: Look back at the worked passages and notice where each transition sits and what punctuation follows it.

items.text: We packed our bags. ___, we left for camp.
items.ask: Which transition shows time order?
items.right: We packed our bags. then, we left for camp.
items.hint: Ask whether leaving came after packing or went against it.

items.text: The soup was hot. ___, it was delicious.
items.ask: Which transition fits?
items.right: The soup was hot. in addition, it was delicious.
items.hint: Ask whether being delicious adds to being hot or goes against it.

items.text: The road was closed. Therefore, we took a different route.
items.right: The road was closed. Therefore, we took a different route.
items.label: Cause and effect
items.ask: What does therefore show?
items.hint: Ask how taking a different route connects to the closed road.

card.definition: Coordinating conjunctions join two equal parts of a sentence, such as two words, two phrases, or two complete sentences. The seven are for, and, nor, but, or, yet, and so. The first letters spell FANBOYS.

example.text: Sam wanted to play soccer, but it was raining.
example.note: But joins two complete sentences.

card.how: Look for for, and, nor, but, or, yet, or so between two equal parts. Each one shows a different link, such as adding, contrasting, or choosing.

card.definition: Each FANBOYS conjunction has a job. For gives a reason. And adds. Nor gives a negative choice. But shows a contrast. Or gives a choice. Yet shows a surprising contrast. So shows a result.

example.text: She was hungry, so she ate lunch.
example.note: So shows a result.

more.text: She was hungry, but she waited.
more.note: But shows a contrast.

card.how: Read the two parts the conjunction joins, then ask what link it makes. The link tells you the function.

fanboys-punctuate.title: Punctuating FANBOYS
fanboys-punctuate.ask: Put a comma where one is needed, or say it is right as it is.

card.definition: When a FANBOYS conjunction joins two complete sentences, put a comma before the conjunction. When it joins two words or phrases, do not use a comma.

example.text: Sam wanted to play, but it rained.
example.note: A comma comes before but because two complete sentences are joined.

more.text: Sam wanted to play soccer and basketball.
more.note: No comma, because and joins two words.

card.how: Check both sides of the conjunction. If each side could stand alone as a sentence, add a comma before the conjunction. If not, leave the comma out.

tips.note: Comma before and, two complete sentences.

splices-fused.title: Correcting Comma Splices and Fused Sentences

card.definition: A comma splice joins two complete sentences with only a comma. A fused sentence joins two complete sentences with nothing at all. Both are errors. Fix them with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS conjunction.

example.text: The bell rang, the students left.
example.note: Fused:

then.text: The bell rang the students left.

more.text: The bell rang, so the students left.

card.how: Find the two complete sentences. Then separate them with a period, join them with a semicolon, or join them with a comma and a FANBOYS word.

card.definition: Conjunctive adverbs connect ideas between sentences or clauses. Common ones are therefore, however, also, moreover, furthermore, meanwhile, otherwise, instead, and nevertheless.

example.text: The bus was late. Therefore, we missed the first class.
example.note: Therefore connects the two sentences and shows a result.

card.how: Look for a word that links one sentence to the one before it and shows how the ideas relate, such as a result, a contrast, or an addition.

tips.text: It rained. However, the game went on.
She practiced. Meanwhile, her brother read.
tips.note: Meanwhile shows two things happening at once.

conj-adverbs-middle.title: Punctuating Conjunctive Adverbs in the Middle of a Sentence
conj-adverbs-middle.ask: Put the marks where they go.

card.definition: When a conjunctive adverb sits in the middle of a sentence, put a comma before it and a comma after it. The conjunctive adverb breaks the sentence into two parts and links the ideas.

example.text: The bus was late; therefore, we missed the first class.
example.note: The conjunctive adverb therefore is set off by a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

more.text: We missed the first class, therefore, because the bus was late.
more.note: Commas on both sides set the conjunctive adverb apart.

card.how: A conjunctive adverb in the middle of a sentence needs a comma before it and a comma after it. When it joins two complete sentences, a semicolon comes before it instead of a comma.

tips.text: It rained; however, the game went on.
tips.note: A semicolon comes before however, and a comma comes after it.

card.definition: Subordinating conjunctions join a dependent clause to an independent clause. Common ones are since, when, although, because, if, and while. The group is wider, including after, before, unless, until, and though.

long-short-works.title: Recognizing Titles of Long-Form and Short-Form Works
long-short-works.ask: Is the work long-form or short-form?

card.definition: Long-form works are books, movies, plays, albums, magazines, and newspapers. Short-form works are chapters, poems, songs, articles, and short stories. The kind of work tells you how to format its title.

example.note: is a book, a long-form work.

more.note: is a poem, a short-form work.

card.how: Ask how long the work is and how it is published. A work that stands alone is long-form. A work that appears inside a bigger work is short-form.

choosing-fanboys.title: Using the Appropriate FANBOYS
choosing-fanboys.ask: Press the blank to choose the conjunction that fits.

card.definition: Pick the FANBOYS word that fits the link between the two parts. And adds, but contrasts, or chooses, so shows a result, for gives a reason, nor joins negative choices, and yet shows a surprising contrast.

example.text: She studied hard, so she passed.
example.note: So fits because passing is the result of studying.

more.text: She studied hard, but she was nervous.
more.note: But fits because being nervous contrasts with studying hard.

card.how: Read both parts, ask what link they need, then pick the FANBOYS word that makes that link.

fanboys-errors.title: Correcting FANBOYS Errors
fanboys-errors.ask: Fix the sentence, or say it is right as it is.

card.definition: A FANBOYS error happens when the wrong conjunction is used, or when two complete sentences are joined with a FANBOYS word but no comma. Fix it by picking the right word and adding the comma.

example.text: She was hungry but she waited.
example.note: The word but is right, but the comma is missing. Fixed:

then.text: She was hungry, but she waited.

more.text: It rained, so we played outside.
more.note: The word so is wrong, because playing outside is not a result of rain. Fixed:

then.text: It rained, but we played outside.

card.how: First check the link. Does the conjunction match the link? Then check the punctuation. Two complete sentences need a comma before the conjunction.

tips.note: So fits the result, and the comma is there.

card.definition: Affect is usually a verb. It means to change or influence something. Effect is usually a noun. It means the result of a change.

example.text: The rain will affect our picnic.
example.note: Affect is the verb for changing the picnic.

more.text: The effect of the rain was a wet field.
more.note: Effect is the noun for the result.

card.how: Ask what the word does. Changing or influencing means affect, the verb. The result means effect, the noun.

tips.text: Affect is the action, effect is the end result.
tips.note: A memory trick: affect starts with a, like action.

card.definition: A direct object is the noun or pronoun that receives the action of the verb. It answers the question what or whom after the verb.

conclusion-jobs.title: The Two Jobs of a Conclusion

sections.title: Job one: restate the claim
sections.question: How do I remind the reader what I argued?
sections.body: A conclusion restates the claim in fresh words, so the reader remembers the main point.

passage.label: Claim
passage.text: Schools should keep art classes.

passage.label: Conclusion restatement
passage.text: Art classes belong in every school.

sections.note: The idea is the same, but the words are new.

sections.title: Job two: leave a final thought
sections.question: What should the reader take away?
sections.body: A conclusion ends with a final thought that gives the reader something to remember, such as a call to action or a look ahead.

passage.text: If we protect art classes now, the next generation of artists, builders, and thinkers will thank us.

sections.note: The final thought looks ahead and gives the reader a reason to care.

sections.title: What a conclusion does not do
sections.question: What should I avoid?
sections.body: A conclusion should not bring in new evidence, start a new argument, or repeat the essay word for word.

passage.text: Art classes are good.
Art classes are good.
Art classes are good.

sections.note: This repeats the same words and adds nothing new, so it fails both jobs.

card.definition: A contraction joins two words with an apostrophe and leaves out letters. A possessive shows ownership and usually uses an apostrophe too, but it does not join two words.

sections.title: What a counterargument is
sections.question: What would someone who disagrees say?
sections.body: A counterargument is the strongest point on the other side. Naming it shows the writer has thought about both sides.

passage.label: Claim
passage.text: School should start later.

passage.label: Counterargument
passage.text: Some people say a later start would push sports and jobs into the evening.

sections.note: This names the other side's best point.

sections.title: How to answer it
sections.question: How do I respond without dismissing the other side?
sections.body: A good response takes the counterargument seriously and answers it with a fact or a reason.

passage.text: Sports can end a little later, and studies show that rested students learn more, so the trade is worth it.

sections.note: The response respects the concern and answers it with a fact.

sections.title: Where it belongs
sections.question: Where does the counterargument paragraph go?
sections.body: It usually comes after the main reasons and before the conclusion, so the writer answers the other side and then ends strong.

passage.text: Some people worry about evening sports.
Still, the gain in learning is greater than the change in schedule, so a later start is the better choice.

sections.note: The paragraph answers the concern and leads into the conclusion.

verb-tenses.title: Identifying Verbs in Simple, Progressive, and Perfect Tenses

card.definition: Verbs change form to show time. Simple tenses show one time: past, present, or future. Progressive tenses show an action in progress, using a form of be plus ing. Perfect tenses show an action finished before another time, using a form of have plus a past participle.

example.text: She walked.
example.note: Simple past.

more.note: Present progressive, an action in progress.
Present perfect, an action finished before now.

card.how: Look at the verb form. The main verb alone, or will plus the verb, means simple. A form of be plus ing means progressive. A form of have plus a past participle means perfect.
